pages.text: The $(item)Radio Telescope$() is a dish on an alt-azimuth mount with a $(item)Feed Horn$() at its focus. Radio passes through cloud and daylight: it works at any hour, rain or shine - but it needs a view of the sky, and every machine running within 24 blocks is $(thing)noise$() in its receiver.

A source raises the antenna temperature by T = S·A/2k; the receiver hears it over the system temperature, T_sys. Taking in a band B for a time τ beats the noise down: $(thing)SNR = T·√(Bτ)/T_sys$(). The Galaxy itself roars at low frequencies, so T_sys climbs steeply below a few hundred MHz.

$(thing)Hydrogen$() glows in a narrow line at 1420.4 MHz. Tune to it and keep the band narrow: a line half a megahertz wide is diluted in a wider one. $(thing)Pulsars$() are faint and broadband - take a wide band for the SNR, but not so wide that dispersion in the interstellar plasma, 8.3 µs·DM·B/ν³, smears the pulse beyond a millisecond. Higher frequencies smear less, but the pulsar is fainter there.

Every map and timing record gives $(thing)Insight$(). Once you have mapped how fast the Galaxy turns, the long galactic survey gives a great deal more - and a $(thing)binary pulsar$() can be timed: its orbit shrinks exactly as general relativity predicts, measured against a $(item)Time-Dilated Sample$() as the reference clock.
